CookieRun: Crumble

CRC · Eden of Gaming Hub

CookieRun: Crumble

Overview
Live Patch 1.0 Launch week meta

Eden of Gaming has run top-ranked gacha guilds since 2018 and is potentially the highest-power English-speaking guild in CookieRun: Crumble today. Crumble takes the franchise into idle RPGs: a twelve-Cookie squad that fights without you, 70 Cookies across six rarity grades, five elements, seven Synergies, and an offline Auto Hunt clock that decides how fast you progress. Live July 30, with Cool Mint Cookie added on August 13; this hub covers the meta from inside the game.

2 coupon codes are live for CookieRun: Crumble. Codes are redeemed on the official web page rather than inside the game, and the reward only appears after you restart the game.

How to redeem

  1. Open the official coupon page. Redemption happens on the web, not in the game.
  2. Find your MID. In game, open the Menu on the right of the main screen, go into Settings, and read it under User Info. It is five letters and four digits, like PHDLZ5054. There is no sign-in and no password: the form is anonymous, and the account field also accepts the email bound to the account, or a guest MID in the form GUEST-XXXXX00000.
  3. Paste the code. It is not case-sensitive, the field upper-cases whatever you type, and each code works once per account.
  4. Restart the game. The reward lands in your mailbox, which itself only unlocks after the Clear Stage 2-1 quest, so a brand-new account has to play a little before it can collect.

The two rules the developer prints on the form:

  • Each Coupon Code can be used only once per account.
  • To receive the reward, restart the game after entering the Coupon Code.

If a code fails, the message tells you which problem you have. "Please check the coupon code" means no such code exists, usually a typo. "This coupon code is currently not available, please check the coupon code usage dates" means the code is real but outside its window. "This coupon code has already been used" is self-explanatory, and it is once per account rather than once per device.

A guest account can redeem: the coupon form takes a guest MID directly. Bind the account anyway. The English App Store listing warns in as many words that guest data is lost if you uninstall, and no coupon reward survives that.

Expired

No Crumble code has expired yet. Both live codes were announced on the official Korean cafe, which is the only channel that has ever carried one, and nothing else has been issued since launch.

Why this list is short

Codes for Crumble come from the official Korean cafe and social channels, in-game news and the official Discord. Every code list published before July 30 was fabricated, because the game did not exist yet and no codes had been issued. EOG lists a code here only when it comes from the developer or from someone in the network who has actually redeemed it.

Both live codes were announced only on the official Korean channels and both celebrate Korean store milestones, but the coupon form is served in five languages against one backend and no region restriction is stated on either announcement. The developer has not said either way, so neither has EOG.

Patch 1.1, first content update · Updated August 13, 2026 · Kit-derived

The boards

Most Cookies need 5 stars to shine, so both boards are ranked on a 5-star default. Play around with what works for you and your own star levels. Vetted by Akram, Lineve and Chuong.

EOG's launch-week PvE read from our Server 1 Rank 1 push, ranked for waves across Stages, Crumble Dungeon and Plaque Tower, and folding in the sub-SSR Cookies a top squad actually fields, not just the high-rarity pool. Tap any Cookie for the reasoning. The pill on each card is a separate read on how much outside sources agree about the kit, not the tier.

Cookies

The poison-comp core the whole PvE meta is built on: the carry plus the multipliers that scale it

S Build around

Clear speed, a free-account floor, a multiplier the rest of the squad rides on, or the concentrated damage the Dungeon and Tower bosses ask for

B Situational

Playable, unremarkable, or waiting on a number the game does not print

Three Pet slots, ranked for waves. Only an equipped Pet applies its Companion Effect, so this is a contest between Companion Effects and nothing else. Passive Effects apply from the bench and are a reason to collect rather than a reason to equip.

Send us a build. Make it in the Build Maker, hit Copy Link, and post it in the CookieRun: Crumble channel on the EOG Discord. Anything that holds up gets published here with your name on it. No reader submissions yet, so the list below is EOG lineups only.

Every build here is credited to a named player and carries a link you can load and edit. There are no scores or vote counts: with a roster this size a handful of votes would be noise, and nothing on the page is worth more for having been clicked. The gold badge means an EOG analyst has fielded or checked the lineup, and it is the only quality claim made. On the Applications count. Read it as coverage, not as a damage figure. Synergies do not appear in the damage formula at all: a step raises a number on the skill itself, and which number depends on the Synergy. Volley adds projectiles and Rapid Fire adds activations, so those two behave close to a straight damage multiplier on a single target. Pierce, Chain and Range add targets, which is worth a great deal in a crowd and nothing against one boss. Projectile Speed and Duration buy consistency rather than damage. Two builds on the same Applications total can therefore be doing very different things, and a boss lineup should be judged on the first pair rather than on the total.

Crumble Dungeon: the Cookies to take out

Patch 1.1 · Updated August 14, 2026 · EOG testing

The Dungeon fields your top 40 by Combat Power, so lower the levels on everything you do not want in there. Every other mode in Crumble is a formation you choose. The Dungeon is not. It throws your whole collection at the Holy Golden Drop, scores you on total damage, and decides the running order itself: strongest first by Combat Power, top 40 to the front. Those 40 are the Cookies on the field while your buffs are up.

40

Cookies deployed first, ranked by Combat Power

Higher

the level your 40 have to sit at against everything else

Combat Power comes from level, and level is the one thing you control. That makes the whole tech straightforward. Lower the EXP on the Cookies below until they drop under the 40th-place cutoff, and your best units move up to take the places they were occupying. You are not deleting anything, you are making room.

What that buys you is control of your supports. In this mode you cannot aim a heal or a buff, and the game does not allocate them by who is dealing the damage. It allocates them by which allied body is hurt and by which allied body carries a matching Synergy tag. Neither of those is your carry. Every Cookie on the list below is a body that wins one of those allocations and then converts it into nothing.

+42%

from benching two of the best Cookies in the game

The controlled test this rests on

We ran the same account twice on August 13 and kept both result screens. With a 10-star Oven Wanderer Cookie and a 10-star Cool Mint Cookie in the lineup it scored 403,708,109. With both benched it scored 574,531,356.

  • It tests the divers and the summoners. It does not test the Projectile Speed group at all.
  • Cool Mint was left in the Leader slot on the second run by mistake, with no tickets left to redo it, so the real ceiling is probably higher.
  • It is one account on one day. Three attempts on a second and younger account showed no change at all, which we put down to a flatter levelling curve there, and that has not been confirmed.

How to do it

  1. Sort your collection by Combat Power and find where 40th place falls. That line is your Dungeon lineup.
  2. Lower the levels on anything from the list below until it drops under that line, which frees the slots for your best units to move up into.
  3. Nothing needs to go to level 1, and there is no level to aim for, because the cutoff moves with your account. Keep the 40 you want deployed levelled above everything else and that is the whole rule. The job is a chore and there is no way around that.
This is not free, and we will say so outright: three of the Cookies you are benching are genuinely strong. Ion Cookie Robot, Oven Wanderer Cookie and Licorice Cookie are the ones that hurt to lose. Do it if you are chasing a record. The Dungeon settles its ranking daily and runs are ticket-limited, so testing it on your own account is slow.

The 15 Cookies to keep out of your top 40

Three groups, and they are not equally well evidenced. Each one states what backs it and where it stops, because two of them rest on a mechanic the game corroborates and the third rests on a reading we have not been able to confirm.

The ones that charge in

Cookies whose skill carries them into the enemy

Best evidenced of the three, and half of the tested A to B swing

A Cookie that dives at the boss is the Cookie taking the damage, which makes it the lowest-HP ally on the field. Heals and shields go to the lowest-HP ally, so the divers drink the sustain your carries were supposed to get.

The second half is positional. The supports follow the divers forward, which walks the buffs out of range of the ranged damage dealers standing behind.

What backs it up

The targeting key is not a guess. Ion Cookie Robot's own skill line, printed on its card, says it shields itself and the lowest-HP ally, so the game does select on current HP.

Where it stops

Treat the six as the current output of the rule rather than as a closed set: it is what we have tested, not a census. Class is not the test either, since two of the six are Tanks and Strawberry Shortcake is a Charge Cookie we tested and cleared.

  • Oven Wanderer Cookie

    TSSR · Fire · Charge

    Confirmed, and one of the two Cookies in the score test

    Its card has it charge the highest-ATK enemy and collide with everything on the way.

  • Ion Cookie Robot

    SSR · Water · Tank

    Confirmed

    Charges in, then shields itself and the lowest-HP ally, which is the same rule the tech is exploiting.

  • Schwarzwalder

    SSR · Fire · Tank

    Confirmed

    Leaps in and slams, then stays in the boss's face at low HP. Note the name: this is Schwarzwalder, not Muscle Cookie.

  • Peach Cookie

    SR · Fire · Charge

    Observed once, not retested

    She throws herself forward and falls over backwards. No card text has been recorded for her.

  • Poison Mushroom Cookie

    R · Dark · Charge

    Weakest entry on this board, observed once and never retested

    We are least sure of this one and would rather say so than pad the list.

  • Skater Cookie

    C · Water · Charge

    Observed once, not retested

    No card text has been recorded for her either.

The ones that receive Projectile Speed

Every Cookie that receives the Projectile Speed Synergy, except Milk

The weak leg. Real list, and a reason we cannot confirm

The reason we have is that Pomegranate Cookie's buff beam chooses who it lands on by Synergy match first and Combat Power only second, so any Projectile Speed Cookie in the top 40 intercepts the biggest team buff in the game no matter how useless it is.

That is a reading, not a rule of the game, and we will not dress it up as one. It assumes the beam lands on a limited set, and our own record of Pomegranate says the opposite twice: Skill AMP plus 46.5 percent to the team, measured at plus 0.60 to every ally. If the buff really is team-wide then nothing can be intercepted and this group does nothing. We have not run a score test on this group by itself.

What backs it up

The membership is solid even though the reasoning is not. The in-game Synergy panel lists eight Cookies on its Projectile Speed recipients tab, these seven and Milk, and our own dex independently returns the same eight.

Where it stops

Do not de-level Pomegranate Cookie herself. She grants Projectile Speed, she does not receive it, and benching her is the single most expensive mistake available on this page. Note also that Alchemist Cookie grants it too.

  • Madeleine Cookie

    SSR · Light · Tank

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

  • Cream Soda Cookie

    SSR · Water · Charge

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

  • Strawberry Shortcake Cookie

    SSR · Grass · Charge

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

    Here for the Synergy only. We tested her separately and she does not charge in, so she is not a body-slammer.

  • Lemon Cookie

    SR · Light · Ranged

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

  • Blackberry Cookie

    R · Dark · Charge

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

  • Cocoa Cookie

    R · Water · Tank

    From the in-game Synergy panel, and the clearest case of the seven

    Comes out purely because she is Projectile Speed. Nothing else about her is the problem.

  • Zombie Cookie

    U · Grass · Tank

    From the in-game Synergy panel, Projectile Speed recipients

The ones that summon

Cookies that put an extra allied body on the field

Same mechanic as the divers, and the other half of the tested swing

A summoned minion counts as an ally, so your healers walk off and heal the summons instead of your damage dealers. It is the same failure as the divers from the other end: the divers give the healers a hurt body to chase, the summoners give them extra bodies to chase.

What backs it up

Cool Mint Cookie is the half of the score test that can be checked against her card, which does say she summons skulls out of the ground she digs up. She was a prediction before she launched, and the score test the next night confirmed it.

Where it stops

The claim is about healing only. Nothing shows that summons dilute Pomegranate's buff or any other effect, so do not extend it. This group also cannot be extended by reading cards: Milky Way Cookie's card says it summons a dream train, and Milky Way is one of our own keepers.

  • Licorice Cookie

    SR · Dark · Tank

    Confirmed by watching healers walk to its summons

    Its card has never been transcribed, so the summon rests on that observation. One of the three losses that actually hurt.

  • Cool Mint Cookie

    SSR · Water · Charge

    Predicted before launch, then confirmed by the score test

    The Dungeon is the one place the Cookie this hub ranks A for PvE is actively worth benching.

Keep these in

The three that get benched by mistake.

Milk Cookie's Crunchy Strong Pediatrician

The stated exception

She receives Projectile Speed like the other seven and she stays in anyway, which is the one place this rule bends. The reason is that none of the carries can even receive Projectile Speed: Wind Archer takes Pierce, Milky Way takes Range, Melon Soda takes Rapid Fire, and Scorpion takes Volley and Duration. Milk is the only place the beam has to go, so she is the intended destination rather than an exception to the rule.

Nameless Cake Hound

Taken back off the list

It was on the first cut of this list and came off the next day. It gets confused with Oven Wanderer Cookie, which is the actual body-slammer. Its card has it swing a blade where it stands rather than travel, which fits the exemption.

Pomegranate Cookie

Never de-level her

She is the reason the second group exists. She grants Projectile Speed rather than receiving it, and the buff being fought over is hers. Benching her removes the thing the whole group is trying to protect.

Where this comes from, and how long it will last

This is EOG Dungeon testing, run on our own accounts between August 12 and 13, 2026, and published first here. The developer has disclosed nothing about any of it, so everything below is observation rather than documentation, and the parts we have not settled are listed above rather than smoothed over.

Working as of August 14, 2026. Treat it as temporary: this is a design fault rather than a feature, and we expect it to be corrected.

Sugar Rune tiers

Which of the 14 rune lines to actually chase. Three general boards first, one per role, then a ladder of its own for the 25 Cookies whose kit changes the answer. Every placement carries its reason: tap a chip to read it.

The board 45 of the 70 Cookies craft off, including 9 of the 13 Tanks, because what a Cookie is for matters more here than what its class is called.

S Chase these

Skill Haste. Casts per second scale as 1 plus haste over 100, so point for point it is worth exactly what Skill Amplification is worth, and it raises the whole skill at once rather than one term of it. The damage of a Cookie that fights on its own is a rate, not a hit, and this is the only line that moves the rate. It is also the rarest in the pool by a factor of twenty, 1 in 261 against 1 in 13, so a slot holding it is the last one to overwrite.

A Strong

Skill Amplification. Its own multiplicative bucket, and it multiplies a skill's whole output rather than only its damage, so a heal or a buff the kit hands out scales with it too. Equal to Skill Haste per point on the damage maths and twenty times easier to roll, at 1 line in 13, which is what makes it the one you actually build toward. It reaches the skill and nothing else.

ATK Amplification. Multiplies the Attack stat itself, before the damage product starts, so it sits under every number the Cookie produces: basic attacks and skills alike, where Skill Amplification reaches the skill only. Nothing about it is conditional and nothing about it decays.

B Worth a slot

CRIT DMG. The crit bucket is 1 plus stacks times CRIT DMG, and expected stacks are your crit rate, so this pays only in proportion to the CRIT% standing behind it. Half of a pair, which is what keeps the pair behind the amps.

CRIT%. Never wasted, even past 100 percent: every full 100 becomes a guaranteed extra crit stack and each stack applies another full CRIT DMG. Still half of a pair, so it is worth exactly as much as the CRIT DMG it has to multiply.

C Only once the above is done

DMG Reduction. A straight percentage off incoming damage, unconditional, and it multiplies with the other defensive factors rather than adding to them. It buys uptime, which is not damage but is not nothing either.

HP Amplification. The one defensive stat with no diminishing return and no counter-stat. Every point is a point, and a dead damage dealer deals none.

D Everything else

Accuracy Amplification. Hit chance is your Accuracy over enemy Avoidance, clamped at 100 percent. Under the bar every miss loses the whole swing, damage and debuff together; at the bar every further point is inert. It is a threshold to clear, and a rune slot is an expensive way to clear it.

Focus Rate. Conditional, and the condition is binary. Nothing at all on a Cookie that applies no debuff, and among the strongest lines in the game on one that does, because a debuff's listed chance runs through your Focus over enemy Resist and enemy Resist climbs 10.2 times across the campaign. It sits here because most Cookies fail the condition, and it leads the ladder on the ones that meet it.

DEF Amplification. Mitigation is logarithmic with a constant of 500, so 500 DEF cuts 41 percent and 1,000 reaches only 52. It decays faster than either of the other two defensive lines.

Evasion Amplification. A dodged hit takes nothing at all, but it contests enemy Accuracy, and enemy Accuracy reaches 16.6 times base by the last chapter. It thins out exactly where the campaign gets hard.

Movement SPD. A flat constant, and absent from every term in the damage formula. Positioning utility only.

Resistance Rate. Answers enemy Focus, and enemy Focus never moves off 1.0 across all 9,840 stages through 328-30, while their Accuracy, Avoidance and Resist all climb. There is nothing in the campaign for this to resist. The reading once stopped at 168-30, and a rate export covering the full ladder confirmed the later chapters are flat too.

CRIT RES. Lowers the crit chance of whoever is attacking you. No monster carries any CriticalResist, and neither do Arena or Clash bots, so it never touches anything you are shooting at. Defensive, and only against a real player.

Holds the front. Runes buy output rather than padding, because the class already brings the largest HP and DEF pools in the game before a rune touches them.

S Chase these

Skill Haste. A taunt, a shield or an aura protects only while it is up, so cooldown is uptime and uptime is the job. Cooldown is base times 100 over haste plus 100, and nothing else on the board shortens the window where the front line is holding nothing.

A Strong

ATK Amplification. A tank kit is still measured in numbers, and ATK Amplification is under all of them: the hit it does deal, and on a kit whose heal is written as a percentage of Attack, that too. It multiplies the Attack stat before anything else in the product touches it.

Skill Amplification. On a tank this is a defensive stat. It multiplies a skill's whole output rather than only its damage, so a damage-reduction aura grows with it exactly as a hit does, and that half is measured rather than assumed. Scope it: shields are the one output not named on the in-game Stats screen, so on a pure shield kit read this as likely rather than proven.

B Worth a slot

HP Amplification. No diminishing return, no counter-stat, every point a point, and on the kits whose shield is written off their own HP it is the size of the shield rather than a survival stat. It sits behind the output lines only because the class already brings the largest HP pool in the game before a rune touches it.

DMG Reduction. A straight percentage off everything incoming, and it multiplies with Defence rather than adding to it, so it keeps paying at the point where DEF has flattened out.

C Everything else

CRIT DMG. Pays on the damage the kit does deal, and only in proportion to the CRIT% behind it.

CRIT%. Same half-of-a-pair problem, with less damage on a tank for it to land on. Crit past 100 percent is still not wasted: each full 100 is another guaranteed stack.

Accuracy Amplification. A taunt still has to connect, so the stage bar applies here too. Clear it, do not stack it.

Focus Rate. Conditional, and tanks meet the condition more often than the class suggests, since a taunt, a stun and a DEF Down are all applied effects. Where the kit is built on one it leads that Cookie's own ladder, because Focus over enemy Resist decides whether the effect lands at all and enemy Resist reaches 1,020 by the last stage.

DEF Amplification. Real, and logarithmic: 500 DEF is a 41 percent cut and 1,000 only reaches 52. Because the three defensive factors multiply, a spread across them beats a pile into this one.

Evasion Amplification. A dodged hit takes nothing at all, but enemy Accuracy reaches 16.6 times base by the last chapter, so it thins out exactly when the front line is under the most pressure.

Movement SPD. Repositioning only, and absent from every damage term.

Resistance Rate. Answers enemy Focus, and enemy Focus never moves off 1.0 across all 9,840 stages through 328-30, while their Accuracy, Avoidance and Resist all climb. There is nothing in the campaign for this to resist. The reading once stopped at 168-30, and a rate export covering the full ladder confirmed the later chapters are flat too.

CRIT RES. Lowers the crit chance of whoever is attacking you. No monster carries any CriticalResist, and neither do Arena or Clash bots, so it never touches anything you are shooting at. Defensive, and only against a real player.

Buffs, heals and Synergy grants. Two things decide the value and neither is damage: how often the skill goes off, and how large the effect is when it does.

S Chase these

Skill Haste. Cooldown is base times 100 over haste plus 100, so on a support this is uptime on the effect itself, and a buff nobody is standing under is worth nothing however large it is. It is the one line on this board that is never conditional on what the kit does. It does have an end: a 9 second buff on a 10 second cooldown needs about 12 haste to never drop, and past that point further Haste on that Cookie does nothing at all, which is why the permanent-uptime buffers invert this on their own ladder.

A Strong

Skill Amplification. Measured, not inferred. The caster's own Skill AMP multiplies the buff it hands out, so a Cookie dealing no damage whatsoever still scales every point of it: on Pomegranate Cookie each point reached every ally at 0.60, against 1.00 for the same point rolled on a single carry. Healing is named on the same first-party screen. Unlike Haste it has no ceiling, which is what carries it past Haste on a Cookie whose buff is already up.

ATK Amplification. Support output is written off the caster's Attack where a card shows the working: Herb Cookie's heal is 33.3 percent of ATK. On a healer this is the heal stat, not a damage stat, which is why the healers rank it here or higher on their own ladders. Check the card before committing the slot, because a buffer that grants a flat stat gets nothing from it.

B Worth a slot

HP Amplification. A support that dies stops supporting, and none of what it does is conditional on dealing damage.

DMG Reduction. Keeps the kit running through the damage that kills a back line, and multiplies with the other defensive factors rather than adding to them.

C Everything else

CRIT DMG. Only on the damage portion of the kit, if there is one, and only in proportion to the CRIT% behind it.

CRIT%. Same, on whatever damage the kit happens to deal.

Accuracy Amplification. Only matters where the kit has to land a hit to do its work. A threshold to clear, not a line to stack.

Focus Rate. Conditional, and this is the role most likely to meet the condition. A support built around applying a debuff wants Focus above an enemy Resist that reaches 1,020 by the final stage against a base of 100, and those Cookies carry their own ladder.

DEF Amplification. Survivability on the logarithmic curve, useful in combination with the other two defensive factors rather than in bulk.

Evasion Amplification. A losing race against an enemy Accuracy that reaches 16.6 times base in the late campaign.

Movement SPD. Positioning only, and absent from every damage term.

Resistance Rate. Answers enemy Focus, and enemy Focus never moves off 1.0 across all 9,840 stages through 328-30, while their Accuracy, Avoidance and Resist all climb. There is nothing in the campaign for this to resist. The reading once stopped at 168-30, and a rate export covering the full ladder confirmed the later chapters are flat too.

CRIT RES. Lowers the crit chance of whoever is attacking you. No monster carries any CriticalResist, and neither do Arena or Clash bots, so it never touches anything you are shooting at. Defensive, and only against a real player.

The other 25 rank their own, and their first craft is the gold line on the tile. Tap any Cookie for the full ladder, the reasoning and the real craft odds.

The rules behind the tiers

Skill Haste leads all three boards

It is the only line whose worth does not depend on what the kit is for. A shorter cooldown pays a carry, a healer, a shield tank and a stunner in exactly the same way, because every one of them is standing around waiting on the same timer, and a Cookie that fights on its own produces a rate rather than a hit. Cooldown is base times 100 over haste plus 100, so casts per second scale as 1 plus haste over 100, which makes it worth precisely what Skill Amplification is worth per point on damage while also raising every other thing the skill does. Supply is the second half. At 1 line in 261 against 1 in 13 for everything else, you will not assemble a board of it, so the ranking is really an instruction about what to keep: when a craft hands you Haste, that slot is finished.

Skill Haste and Skill Amplification are the same mechanic

One raises damage per cast, the other raises casts per second, and the maths makes them equal point for point, which is why they sit in neighbouring tiers rather than opposite ends of the board. Where they part is ceiling and supply. Haste stops paying the moment the effect never drops, roughly 12 haste for a 9 second buff on a 10 second cooldown, and that ceiling is exactly why six Cookies below invert the pair on their own ladder. Skill Amplification never reaches one, and it appears on 1 line in 13 against Haste at 1 in 261, so it is the one you can actually build toward. Craft for Amplification because you can, and take Haste whenever a roll hands it over.

ATK Amplification is under everything, which is why it never misses

It multiplies the Attack stat itself, before the damage product starts. That puts it beneath every number the Cookie produces, basic attacks and skills together, where Skill Amplification and Skill Haste reach the skill and stop. Nothing about it is conditional, nothing about it decays, and no enemy stat contests it. That is the argument for it sitting level with Skill Amplification on every board and being the one offensive line that is never dead on any kit, healers included, where it is buying heal size rather than damage.

Skill Amplification scales buffs and heals, not only damage

The in-game Stats screen says a skill's damage, healing and buff effect all move with it, and the buff half is measured rather than assumed. Adding Skill AMP to Pomegranate Cookie in four steps raised the Skill AMP her buff granted an ally by exactly 0.60 per point every time, which is the caster's own Skill AMP multiplying the buff's base value the same way it multiplies a damage skill's coefficient. Two things follow. It is live on a Cookie that deals no damage at all, so it is never dead on a support. And on a buffer it is worth more than on a carry, because the point spreads across everybody the buff touches instead of landing on one Cookie.

On a healer, ATK Amplification is a healing stat

Herb Cookie's card is the one heal in the roster printed in full, and it reads 33.3 percent of ATK over six healing counts. A heal is written as a percentage of the caster's Attack, so on the healers, Herb, Toothpaste and Milk Pediatrician among them, ATK Amplification is buying heal size rather than damage. That is why three Supports rank a damage stat above Skill Amplification or level with it, and why Milk Pediatrician pulls it all the way up beside Skill Haste. Scope it: one card is the whole evidence base, so treat it as the reading the roster supports rather than a published rule, and check the card of any healer you are gearing.

Focus Rate is why 25 Cookies have their own list

A debuff's listed chance is not its real chance. It runs through your Focus Rate over the enemy's Resistance, and enemy Resistance climbs from 100 to 1,020 across the campaign while nothing else about the debuff changes. On a Cookie that applies nothing, Focus is the deadest stat on the board. On a Cookie whose whole skill is a stun, a transform or a DEF shred, it decides whether the skill happens at all, and every other stat is multiplying a number that may never land. There is no middle: it is bottom-tier on all three general boards, ranked on eight Cookies and first on two of them, and the only thing that moves it is reading the card.

CRIT% and CRIT DMG are a product, not a ladder

The crit multiplier is 1 plus stacks times CRIT DMG, and expected stacks are just your crit rate. That makes the pair a product, so the marginal value of each depends on how much of the other you already hold, and a slot spent on one of them alone buys the least of any offensive line on the board. Stack whichever you are shorter of. The unusual part is that crit rate past 100 percent is not wasted: every full 100 becomes a guaranteed extra stack, so there is no cliff to stop at.

The defensive stats multiply, so spread them

Defence, element resistance and DMG Reduction are separate factors in the damage product, not entries in a sum. Two 40 percent cuts give 0.6 times 0.6, a 64 percent reduction, not 80. Combined with DEF being logarithmic against a constant of 500, a spread across the three always beats an overinvestment in one, and it is why HP Amplification and DMG Reduction are the two that get ranked while DEF Amplification is left to gear.

Accuracy is a bar, not a stat to scale

Hit chance is your Accuracy divided by enemy Avoidance and clamped at 100 percent. Under the bar you are throwing away whole swings, damage and debuffs together, because a miss never reaches the damage roll. At the bar you hit every time and every further point is inert. Look up the bar for the stage you are pushing, clear it from gear, and do not spend a rune line on it.

Two stats do nothing in the campaign at all

Resistance Rate answers enemy Focus, and enemy Focus never moves off 1.0 across all 9,840 stages through 328-30, while their Accuracy, Avoidance and Resist all climb. CRIT RES lowers the crit chance of whoever is attacking you, and no monster, Arena bot or Clash bot carries any. Neither is a bad stat so much as an inert one across the whole campaign, and the game gives you no way to work that out.

These boards are EOG's own. The game publishes no rune tier list, and no in-game screen states what any of these 14 stats is worth, so the ranking is a judgement and the reason is attached to every line for you to disagree with. What the game does publish is the craft table, which is why every percentage on this page is exact even where the ordering is not. Two placements rest on measurement rather than argument: Skill Amplification multiplying the buff a caster grants, from a controlled in-game test on August 10, 2026, and Herb Cookie's heal reading as 33.3 percent of ATK on an English card, which is what has ATK Amplification ranked as a healing stat rather than a damage one on three Supports. One limit worth stating plainly. A ladder is only as good as what is known about the kit under it, and skill text has been transcribed for 24 of the 70 Cookies, so 14 of the 25 own ladders carry no card you can check them against, and each of those cards says so. And these are craft priorities rather than a build: the best roll in the pool is 0.0077 percent, so craft for the stat and take the tier you are given.

Cookie and Pet art: Devsisters. Every portrait was checked against that Cookie's in-game catalogue card before publishing. Returning franchise Cookies and all Pets use existing Cookie Run and Cookie Run: Kingdom community-wiki art; five Crumble originals with no franchise equivalent use their in-game summon card, as does the Pet Majestic King Choco Drop, whose card an EOG member screenshotted in-game. Four Crumble-original Pets have no published art and show a monogram tile.

Mixture

Crumble hides its real constraint behind a wall of rarity. Only 18 of the 70 Cookies grant a Synergy, each of them grants exactly one, and most kits are written to scale with a Synergy they cannot supply themselves. Which is why a squad of pulled SSRs routinely loses to a planned squad that happens to include a Rare.

Mixture takes the Cookies you actually own and returns the lineup that switches on the most Synergy for the Cookie you are building around. It is an exact search rather than a ranked list: it evaluates every reachable combination of live Synergies instead of picking the highest tier and hoping.

Always include Nothing pinned

Your roster

Tap a Cookie to toggle whether you own it. Everything starts ticked, so if you are close to a full roster it is faster to drop what you are missing. A red dot marks a Cookie that GRANTS a Synergy, which is the only column that really constrains a lineup.

Owned 70 of 70

Rarity, element, class and both Synergy columns are complete for all 70 Cookies, independently reproduced against a second source. Anything pinned counts as owned whether or not it is ticked.

Why provider access is the whole game

Every kit shows its Synergy-scaled terms on the card, and the game exposes a global Synergy menu with Provider and Recipient tabs, so unlike most launch metas the whole graph is countable in game. Only 18 of the 70 Cookies grant anything, the real scarcity here. Provider access, not rarity, gates your damage. Cool Mint Cookie did not move that number when she arrived: she takes Volley and Duration and supplies neither, which is the majority position on this roster rather than a knock on her.

Provider counts run Range 4, Duration 3, Volley 3, Rapid Fire 2, Projectile Speed 2, Pierce 2, Chain 2, against recipient counts of 18, 15, 10, 12, 8, 6 and 5. Every Cookie in the game receives something, so the whole roster is waiting on those eighteen. Chain and Pierce are the pinch points at two Cookie providers each, and in Pierce's case the pairing with Wind Archer is close to a hard dependency rather than a preference. Pets partly cover the gap and do it by adding flat magnitude rather than switching a Synergy on: Fluffy Cheese Cat reads "Ally Chain Synergy +1", Furball Pup "+30% Projectile Speed". They are not in this solver because they occupy their own three slots rather than lineup slots.

Granting and receiving are separate tags, so a provider almost never benefits from its own Synergy. Exactly one Cookie in the game does: Knight Cookie, an Uncommon, both grants and receives Range.

Coverage is necessary, not sufficient

One caution the solver cannot model. Synergy is not a lineup-wide flag: it is granted by the provider's active skill, on a cooldown, for a few seconds at a time, and nine of the eighteen providers only reach allies inside the skill's radius. So coverage is necessary, not sufficient. A lineup that switches on seven Synergies still needs its Cookies bunched together in the fight for most of them to land, which is the real reason positioning matters in this game.

Stellar Link planner

Stellar Link is the one place in Crumble where position provably pays. Twelve slots sit around a ring, your Star Shards drop into them at random, and the game draws a link from shard one to shard two, on to the last, and back to the first. The area that closed shape encloses amplifies the attack, defence and health of every Cookie in your lineup, so two boards holding identical shards can be worth wildly different amounts purely on the order they landed in.

Tap the slots below in the order your shards landed, exactly as the board reads in game. The planner returns the area you are on, the ceiling for that shard count, which shards to lock, and what finishing from here should cost. Locking is the entire game: it is the only control you get over a system that is otherwise pure chance.

What the developer has actually said

The developer says four things about this board and nothing else. How many placements exist at each shard count. That every placement is equally likely. That the area and its bonuses are calculated automatically from the shard positions and are not subject to any additional probability. And that locking a shard fixes its position while the unlocked ones reshuffle at random. There is no official statement of what a reset costs, how many locks you get, where the board sits in the menus, what unlocks it, or what the bonus is worth. Everything on this page that is not a percentage was recorded in game.

How to actually run it

Phase 1

Roll naked to roughly 70%

The line sits at roughly 70%: below that there is nothing worth protecting, and an unlocked reset is the cheapest rung on the ladder. Spam it. Locking one shard costs exactly what locking none costs and buys nothing either, because the ring is rotationally symmetric: fixing a single shard only decides where you start reading the board.

Phase 2

Lock as shards land correctly

Once shards start landing in ceiling-correct slots, lock them and step up the ladder. Each lock takes a shard out of the reshuffle, which is the only thing that shortens the odds. The planner tells you which ones are already right, and locking fixes both the slot and the shard order.

Phase 3

Decide whether to chase the last few

At six locks you have spent your control and the rest is chance. With twelve shards and six held, the other six still have to land in the six free slots in exactly one order, which is a one in 720 roll at 220 Stellar Points a go. Most accounts should bank a good board rather than chase a perfect one. The Korean consensus is to settle around 85%.

A reset overwrites the current board and there is no undo, so read the planner before you spend. The area number is worth having, not worth ruining an account over: a board in the mid eighties is a real power gain at a fraction of the cost of a maxed one.

What the board is worth, and what nobody knows

The bonus applies to your whole lineup, and nobody has published what it is worth

Area amplifies attack, defence and health for every Cookie you have fielded. The developer confirms the bonus exists and is deterministic in the shard positions, and publishes no coefficient. Nothing anywhere models the conversion, so the magnitude is not merely undisclosed, it is unknown even where everything else on this page is settled.

Constellations stack, on one source

One Korean tool describes Stellar Link as a sequence of constellations, and reports that the same area is worth more on a higher constellation and that earlier constellation bonuses are kept rather than replaced, which would mean the first board you complete keeps paying. The same source says shard count opens with your active lineup slots on the first constellation and through Cookie promotion after that. Nobody else states any of it, so treat the whole card as a lead rather than a rule.

Where it applies is not settled

One Korean tool states the bonus applies to Main Stage, Crumble Dungeon, Daily Dungeon and Implant Tower, which would exclude the Arena. That is a single unsourced exclusion claim and the developer says nothing about it. Worth knowing before you budget a Stellar Point run around PvP, not worth planning on.

Still open

What unlocks the board, where it sits in the menus, how fast Stellar Points accrue, and what the game does with your placement when the shard count goes up. None of it is documented by anyone, in any language, and this page stays quiet on all four until it is.

The reroll currency is Stellar Points, SP here. The developer uses Stellar Link and Star Shard in English and has never named the currency, so this is the Korean-language term carried over. Launch coupon COOKIERUNCRUMBLE1ST pays 1,000 of them.

Reset cost by locks held

Reset price rises steeply with the number of shards you hold in place. The developer publishes none of these seven figures; they were recorded in game, so treat them as observed rather than official.

LockedReset costWhat it buys
0 locked 10 SP The cheap roll. Everything reshuffles. This is the whole early game.
1 locked 10 SP Same price as rolling naked and the same result, because the ring looks identical from every angle. Locking only starts to mean something at two.
2 locked 30 SP Triple the naked price. Worth it once two shards are genuinely in ceiling-correct slots.
3 locked 60 SP Six times naked. The point where a run needs a Stellar Point budget rather than spare change.
4 locked 100 SP Ten times naked. Committed. From here you are buying a specific board, not exploring.
5 locked 150 SP Fifteen times naked. Only correct when five shards are right and you intend to see it through.
6 locked 220 SP The endgame rung, and the one that eats accounts. Six of twelve shards held, and the remaining six still have to land in one exact order.

Ceiling is the most area that many shards can possibly enclose, which is the largest convex shape they can make on the ring. Average deal is what a random board actually gives you, sampled across four hundred thousand simulated deals. Draw simulator

A working model of the Crumble summon screen, running on the official published probabilities rather than an approximation of them. Pick a banner, set your Gacha Level, and draw. It costs nothing and it will not lie to you about the odds.

The reason to use it is not the animation. It is the record underneath: after a few hundred simulated draws you can see how far a real session drifts from a disclosed rate, and how little a ten-draw actually buys at 1.2 percent.

A Pick-up guarantee is widely reported, and nothing has confirmed one.

The Premium pools have no floor at all. A Gacha Lv.9 account reporting 500 draws with no SSR is improbable at roughly 0.3 percent and entirely consistent with the disclosed table, and there is nothing to farm toward. Pick-up is where the disagreement sits. The community figure is one guaranteed copy of the featured Cookie at 180 draws, and 300 on the Pick-up Pet. At 200 Crystals a draw that would put the worst case at 180,000 Crystals. Against that, the pull data itself carries no pity counter and no soft-pity ramp, and explained the guarantee-like feel as a fixed two-weight split that always returns the same probability.

Treat the guarantee as unconfirmed, because the two accounts cannot both be right and neither has been closed out. That check covered the pull weighting rather than everything the game does, so a separate counter is possible, but no evidence of one has been produced. The developer publishes nothing either way, and whether a counter would carry between banners is equally unknown. The simulator still models the reported guarantee, and labels it as reported wherever it appears, so the figure is available without the hub asserting it. Do not commit 180,000 Crystals expecting the game to owe you a Cookie at the end.

The standard Cookie pool, and the only one you can spend freely on. Every launch Cookie is in it, weighted by rank. No guarantee of any kind.

1 Premium Cookie Cutter per draw, or 200 Crystals

Gacha Level

Gacha Level is the largest single lever on what a draw is worth. At Lv.1 the Premium pool is 82 percent Common and 18 percent Uncommon with every other rank at flat zero, SSR is impossible below Lv.4 and TSSR below Lv.6. Spending tickets on a fresh account is not a gamble, it is a guaranteed low-rarity result.

How it rises is not published. It is an experience bar filled by drawing, with a separate level for Cookies and for Pets, capped at Lv.10 and commonly maxed inside the first week. Draws on any Cookie pool feed the same counter, the Special banner included.

TSSR 0.0500% 0.0250% each of 2 SSR 1.20% 0.0571% each of 21 SR 7.00% 0.4667% each of 15 R 13.00% 1.0833% each of 12 U 18.00% 1.6364% each of 11 C 60.75% 6.7500% each of 9

The developer publishes a rate per RANK, not per Cookie. The rank rate is split evenly across everyone in it, so a named SSR at Gacha Lv.10 is 1.2 percent divided by twenty, which is 0.06 percent, one in 1,667 draws. Every Cookie added to the game makes the one you want rarer without any published rate ever changing.

The multi-draw buttons carry no discount and no guaranteed rarity. Ten singles cost exactly what a ten-draw costs and pay exactly the same odds.

Skill Amplification is the strongest stat and it looks the weakest

At every rarity and every tier bar the very bottom one, where it ties, Skill Amplification rolls a smaller number than the stats around it. SSR Tier 01 gives 5.00 where CRIT DMG gives 8.00. That gap is the game pricing it, not undervaluing it. It multiplies a skill's whole output rather than its damage alone, buffs included, so it pays even on a Cookie that never hits anything: a test on August 10, 2026 measured a caster's own Skill AMP raising the Skill AMP its buff granted an ally, at 0.60 per point. Do not skip it because the number is small, and do not skip it on a support.

Skill Haste is the rarest line in the game, not the easiest

The thirteen ordinary stats share one probability per tier. Skill Haste has its own, and at the tiers where it appears it is between 1.25 and 2.7 times the shared rate, which is where the "easy to get" reading comes from. But it only appears on four of the twelve tiers: SSR and SR, tiers 01 and 02. It cannot roll on an R, U or C rune at all. Across the whole pool that puts it at 1 in 261 against 1 in 13 for every other stat. It is the one line worth deliberately crafting for, because you will not stumble into it.

A perfect rune is not a plan

The best roll in the game, SSR Tier 01, sits at 0.007663 percent per stat. That is one craft in thirteen thousand, and there are thirteen stats competing for it. Craft for the stat you need and take the tier you are given. Anyone telling you to reroll for SSR Tier 01 has not read the table.

What the disclosure does not say

  • What a craft costs is not in the article. The probabilities are disclosed because Korean law requires probabilities, not prices.
  • Elemental DMG is not in the rune pool at all. It comes from Pets only, so no amount of crafting will produce it.

The developer rounds every published cell, so the column sums to 100 to four decimal places rather than exactly. That is the disclosure as published, not a transcription error. Pool sums to 100%. Article last updated 2026-07-30.

Stage index

Every stage in the campaign, what waits at the end of it, what that boss is carrying, and, through 168-30, what the stage pays you while you are logged out. The in-game map shows you one stage at a time, never shows the boss stat line at all, and never shows the reward rate, which is the whole reason this exists.

Enter a stage and it returns the boss, how many spawn, the recommended Power, the Accuracy and Focus the stage demands, the boss health, attack and defense, how many kills open the boss fight, and the offline income the stage pays per hour as far as the reward table reaches. Add your own team Power and it also tells you which damage bracket you are standing in and what the next one costs.

Loading the stage tables.

Offline income is a step function, not a curve

Rewards do not rise stage by stage. They hold flat across a band and then jump. Parking one stage below a boundary can cost you a large fraction of your hourly income for no reason at all, so the thing worth checking is not "can I clear this" but "am I sitting just under a step".

Farm the highest stage you have cleared, not the hardest one you can survive

Offline income is paid by the stage you are parked on. Clearing further and then parking further is the entire mechanic, and it is why pushing the campaign beats optimising a team for a wall you cannot pass.

The damage bracket is a ratio, and it is brutal below 10 percent

Under a tenth of the recommended Power you deal 1 percent damage. Reaching a tenth takes you to 5 percent, and the scale climbs from there to 120 percent at 1.2 times recommended. A stage you are far under is not slow, it is arithmetically impossible, and no amount of retrying changes that.

There is no wall at a chapter boundary

Recommended Power never falls and almost never leaps. The largest single step in all 9,839 of them is 1-4 into 1-5, at 1.36 times, and every one of the fifteen biggest sits inside a chapter rather than on its edge. The steepest boundary in the whole game is 1-30 into 2-1 at 1.04 times. If you are stuck, you are stuck on a slot, not on a chapter.

Stage 20 and stage 30 are elite slots, and they hit about three times harder

Both send exactly one body, on all 656 of them, with no exception anywhere in the campaign. Their attack against the recommended Power of the stage they sit in runs about three times what a normal slot in the same chapter carries, on three in four of them, and rarely under double. The one boss that breaks the pattern is GingerCraven, who closes roughly every fourth chapter and hits closer to a normal slot than an elite. Everywhere else, that is where a run ends, and it is why the boss attack column is worth reading before you park.

Past 168-30 the boss outgrows the gate

From 168-30 to 328-30 the recommended Power asks for 79 times more, and the boss brings 183 times the health for it. Attack grows 10 times over and Defense barely moves. Meeting the recommended figure in the late chapters buys you less than the same figure bought you earlier, and the shortfall is health, so it costs you time rather than survival.

Enemy Accuracy stops climbing, and nothing tells you

The Accuracy the enemy brings against your Evasion reaches its ceiling at 168-29 and then holds flat for the final 4,802 stages, nearly half the campaign. The Accuracy a stage demands of you keeps climbing for another eighty chapters past that, to 248-28, before it finds a ceiling of its own; Focus never stops rising at all. Evasion gets quietly better the deeper you go. The bars you have to clear do not, and one of them never stops.

The developer publishes no stage table, no boss list, no boss stat line and no offline reward rate. All of it comes from community play data. The recommended Power column is the part with a check behind it. It reproduces, exactly, every one of the 7,440 figures the hub shipped before this refresh, and the first 3,000 of those were compiled here stage by stage before any community dataset existed, which is the only genuinely independent corroboration the ladder has. Past 168-30 it is a single source. A second file of damage brackets checks out too: all 68,880 of its thresholds reproduce from the recommended figure alone, which is why this tool derives them rather than storing them. Item names marked with a dagger are our rendering of the Korean original, because the English version ships no glossary for them.

A stage checks three numbers against your squad. The Stage Index answers Power. This answers the two the game never explains, and names which of the three actually stops you, because that is the only one worth spending on.

150,000

The total on your Lineup screen. Log-scaled, because the campaign runs from 1,600 to just over 2 billion.

100

Baseline is 100. Focus decides whether your debuffs and disables land at all.

20%

The number printed on the skill, before Focus touches it. Dark Choco's DEF Down is 20 percent.

Resistance is a dead roll in the campaign. Enemy Avoidance runs 1.0 to 12.04 and enemy Resist 1.0 to 11.62 across the full ladder. Enemy Accuracy climbs to 16.62 by 168-29 and then stops, holding flat for the last 4,801 stages. Enemy Focus never moves off exactly 1.0, and that now reads across all 9,840 stages to 328-30 rather than stopping at 168-30. Focus beats their Resist and matters enormously. Resistance would beat their Focus, and nothing in the campaign pushes against it. Scope that to the campaign: this data covers stages only, and a real opponent in the Arena does bring Focus.

Both are modelled, and both formulas are exact rather than fitted to observed behaviour. Hit chance is Accuracy divided by enemy Avoidance, clamped at 100 percent, and enemy Avoidance is 100 times the stage's Avoidance rate, which is the bar in the table above. Debuff rate is the listed chance multiplied by Focus over enemy Resist. One caveat on the Accuracy bar: it assumes the enemy has the standard base Avoidance of 100, true of 154 of the 166 monsters, while seven elites sit at 50 and need only half of it. Source: community data supplied by a player, the same numbers behind the community tool at kopicsiudai.github.io/crumble. Its Power column agrees with the 3,000 stages this hub compiled itself before any community dataset existed, exactly, which is why the two are treated as corroborating each other. A later export carrying the enemy rate columns themselves reproduces all three bars above on every one of the 9,840 stages, so the 1.0 to 100 scale is now checked end to end rather than over the first 5,040.

You do not farm gear in this game. You collect Lucky Dough and a Sugar Gnome rolls equipment out of an Oven, which makes it a third randomized draw sitting behind Cookies and Pets. Unlike those two it is fully countable, because the Oven Level fixes both the rarity odds and the item level.

Every Oven Level's odds sum to exactly 100, which the build asserts.

Package value

Every bundle in the shop, converted to one unit so they can be compared at all. The store shows you one package at a time and never shows you what the last one was worth, which is how a bad deal survives.

Everything a package contains is priced in Crystals, then divided by what the package costs. A draw ticket is worth the Crystals a draw costs. A guaranteed SSR Cookie is worth the 180 draws the Pick-up guarantee takes, because that is the deterministic price of one. The ranking is what matters, not the raw total: bigger packages contain more of everything, so totals only tell you which one is expensive.

Count only what you need
Shop section

Counting 13 of 13 currencies across 57 packages. Best value is Nameless Cake Hound 3-Star Package at 45.25 Crystals per won, which is 20.1 times the median package.

Ranked, best value first

Value is not the same as worth

A package rated highly here is dense in Crystals per unit spent. It is not necessarily a good purchase. A bundle of Pet draws is worthless if your Pets are already built, and duplicates of a Cookie you cannot use are worth nothing whatever the arithmetic says. Use the toggles to count only what you actually need.

Two of the conversions are arguments, not facts

Crystals per draw is observed and solid. Pricing a guaranteed SSR at 180 draws is a defensible choice rather than a published rate, and an SR Cookie is valued at a single draw because nothing exists to price it against, which understates it. Both are stated here rather than buried so you can disagree with them.

Prices are the Korean store in won

That is the catalogue this was read from. It does not weaken the ranking: every storefront prices the same catalogue proportionally, so which package is best is the same everywhere. Read the ordering, not the won figure.

Stage power chart

Damage in Crumble is a ratio, not a flat number. The stage carries a recommended Power figure, your squad is measured against it, and the game pays out a damage percentage off a fixed scale. This chart is that scale for every stage from 1-1 to 328-30, all 9,840 of them.

The useful part is that the scale is the same everywhere. Every threshold is a fixed fraction of the stage's recommended Power: 10% of it puts you in the 5% damage tier, 20% in 15%, 40% in 35%, 60% in 55%, 80% in 75%, the recommended figure itself is 100%, and 120% of it tops the scale out at 120%. Learn that once and you can read any stage in the game without the table.

Damage lab

EOG's own battle model. Put your gear in once and every Cookie in the game is ranked by what its kit actually does at your investment, against the target you pick. Change a number and the order changes with it.

That is the part a tier list cannot do. Crit is worth little on a kit that fires once every eight seconds and a lot on one that fires every two. Skill Haste and Skill AMP trade almost evenly, because haste buys casts rather than bigger hits. Boss DMG is dead weight outside a boss fight. Tap any row for the arithmetic.

Your gear

ATK multiplier is what level, plating, Sugar Runes and Stellar Link have done to a Cookie's base attack. If you do not know it, divide the ATK on any Cookie's profile by its base figure in the roster.

Target

Coefficient bound

16 of the 70 kits have a shape whose single-target hit count cannot be settled from the data: a fan of projectiles that may or may not all reach one body, a Chain bounce that needs a second body to bounce to. Those carry both ends and are marked on the board. The rest are unaffected by this control.

Every Cookie, ranked at your gear

Crumble Dungeon simulator

Crumble Dungeon gives you no controls at all. Your squad is committed, forty Cookies stand on the field, and everything after that is decided by numbers the game never prints: attack range decides which slot a Cookie is placed in, move speed decides when it arrives, and an arena-wide shockwave throws the whole team backwards four times during the run.

The boss then buffs its own damage reduction three times. Reduction in this game screens rather than adds, so those buffs compound instead of capping out, and a run is effectively decided in its first thirteen seconds. That is why a damage-per-second ranking of the roster is the wrong ranking for this mode, and it is the ranking everybody publishes. This tool weights damage against the armour curve instead, so a Cookie that arrives late is scored for arriving late.

Your gear, applied across the lineup

One profile across the whole lineup, because the base stat block is a fixed template per class and nobody gears Cookies differently in practice. What comes out is a ranking of kits at equal investment, which is the comparison worth having. Attack is not in this row: it comes from the level and grade curves below.

Investment

Level and grade both multiply the base stat block, and whether they pool or compound is not settled. At level 100 grade 10 the two readings differ by more than half again, so both are offered and the smaller one leads. Everything in the gear row above is added on top of this.

What to run

Turning effects off is the comparison the rest of this hub could not make before: it is what the lineup scores with every heal, shield, buff and debuff removed and nothing but raw damage left. The gap between the two is what your supports are actually worth.

Slot order

Attack range ascending is the observed rule, and it is a reading rather than a settled fact. The other two are there so you can see how much the uncertainty is actually worth, which for most lineups is very little.

Boss armour, and the coefficient bound

Each boss buff stacks to five and the data states one application per source. Both ends are offered because the accrual rate is not settled. Sixteen kits have a shape whose single-target hit count is not knowable, so those carry a range too.

What this model does not know

    Battle simulator

    Community tool Crumble Battle Simulator built by mokocoder

    This is the one tool on the hub EOG did not build. mokocoder wrote a working model of Crumble combat, and it is the closest thing the game has to a test server: pick a lineup, pick a fight, and watch it resolve. It runs the whole roster, all 70 Cookies and 54 Pets, against every campaign boss.

    The original ships in Korean. It runs here in English, with Cookies, Pets and bosses named the way the rest of this hub names them, so a fight you scout in the Stage Index is spelled the same when you simulate it. Only the wording changed: every number on screen is the simulator's own, and the original is linked below the frame.

    Boss fights

    Run any of the 38 campaign bosses against a 12-slot lineup and watch the fight play back frame by frame.

    Arena matches

    Put two of your own decks against each other on a fixed seed, from both sides, so neither gets the first-strike advantage for free.

    Stage and Arena evaluation

    Batch dozens of runs per deck and rank the results by clear rate, average score and clear time instead of one lucky pull of the RNG.

    Deck manager

    Build and save lineups with level, star grade, Captain, Pets and Mercenary Band perks. Saved in your browser, not on an account.

    Crumble Battle Simulator, English Open in a tab Original
    Loading the simulator. It pulls its engine and sprites on first open, so give it a moment.

    Before you trust a number

    • It is a model of the fight, not the fight. Treat a result as a strong comparison between two lineups rather than a promise about your next run.
    • Every battle is seeded. Change the seed and the same two decks can trade places, which is exactly why the evaluation modes run a deck dozens of times before ranking it.
    • Decks are saved in your browser only. Clearing site data clears them, and they do not follow you to another device.
    • The roster comes from the simulator, not from this hub. If a Cookie shipped this week and the simulator has not picked it up yet, it will not be selectable here either.
    • A few skill and buff lines inside the battle log still read in Korean. Those sit in the simulator engine rather than its interface, and EOG would rather leave a line untranslated than guess at what an effect does and have you build around the guess.

    With thanks to mokocoder

    The simulator is entirely mokocoder's work, built and made public for free. EOG did the English wording and nothing else. If it saves you a bad 12-Cookie investment, that is down to them: the original lives at crumb.run, and they are reachable on Discord as mokocoder.

    The English is ours, so a translation slip is ours too. Report one in the EOG Discord rather than to mokocoder, and we will fix it on our side.

    Skill text for the launch pool is translated from the Japanese version, because that is the only version anyone has written out in full. Two entries are not: Herb Cookie, transcribed off an English card, and Cool Mint Cookie, whose name and card text Devsisters published in English themselves. Names an English-language source also prints are tagged Confirmed, and on the launch pool that tag covers the NAME only: no effect line, number or stat label below it has been read off an English card. Treat a stat name inside a translated line as unverified rather than just differently worded. It has been wrong once already, on Pomegranate Cookie, published here as an ATK buff when the game grants Skill AMP, corrected on August 1, 2026 from a player report. Effect lines describe what the skill does, not how much it does.

    54 Pets at launch, counted in game as SSR 23, SR 12, R 9, U 6, C 4. Four are Crumble originals. The Pet Gacha unlocks at Quest 39, which requires clearing Stage 1-14 by actively summoning that stage's boss. Every Pet carries two effect layers, and the second is the argument for pulling Pets at all: it applies to every Cookie you own, equipped or not. Scope is derived from the effect text, since the developer publishes no scope field.

    Last updated: July 26, 2026 · Written pre-launch · Rarity board, not a tier list

    Rarity is published. Power is not.

    This page was written before launch, when grades were known for all 75 announced Cookies and not one stat, skill or summon rate had been published. It is kept as written, because the rarity board is still the clearest map of how the crossover roster is organized. Since then the live catalogue became readable, so the numbers now exist: the PvE and PvP boards rank the high-rarity pool and the Database carries the stats and skill text. Any CookieRun: Crumble tier list dated before July 30 is still guesswork.

    Crumble is a crossover roster: 75 confirmed Cookies, 64 pulled from a decade of CookieRun history and 11 built new for this game. The organizing idea is Alternative Cookies, and it does more work than it first appears.

    The five elements

    Fire
    Water
    Grass
    Light
    Dark
    Element advantage, from the in-game Stats reference
    ElementDeals more toBonusTakes more fromIts own penalty
    Fire Grass +15% Water no penalty
    Water Fire +15% Grass no penalty
    Grass Water +15% Fire no penalty
    Light Dark +15% Dark no penalty
    Dark Light +15% Light no penalty
    Printed in-game as Fire ← Water ← Grass ← Fire, Light ↔ Dark; arrows point at the element taking extra damage. The Stats screen shows no multiplier, so the +15% and the zero penalty are ours, from testing rather than off any screen. Attacking into a disadvantage is not punished: the last column is empty by design, not because we could not find the number.

    Fire, Water and Grass run the usual three-way loop. Light and Dark are the odd pair: each has advantage over the other in both directions, so a Light Cookie hits a Dark one harder and takes more back, and neither is a safe answer. An advantage is worth plus 15 percent damage, before your own Elemental DMG stat, which adds on top of it. The half nobody expects is the other side: a disadvantage costs you nothing. The inherent penalty is zero, so a bad matchup deals normal damage rather than reduced damage, and the wheel only ever hands out a bonus. That changes how much it is worth building around. Bringing the countering element is a 15 percent gain, not the difference between working and not working, and you never need to avoid a matchup to dodge a penalty that does not exist. The only way a hit lands for less than normal is if the defender has specifically stacked element resistance, which in the campaign they have not. Ignore charts you see elsewhere for this game: they come from Tower of Adventures, which has six elements including Wind and Earth, or from Kingdom.

    Elements are only half of a Cookie card. A second marker sits beside it, a role or position, and the developer has shown exactly one publicly: the summon screen for Oven Wanderer Cookie reads Fire and Charge at TSSR, tagged Alternative. That single card is the entire public sample of how a Cookie gets classified. Until the full role set is published, build for element coverage, not role theory.

    Alternative Cookies

    Alternative is Crumble's headline roster concept: TSSR reimaginings of classic Cookie Run characters from other timelines. Oven Wanderer Cookie is a parallel-universe GingerBrave. GingerCraven is another one, gone bad. Brightseeker Cookie is an older, wearier GingerBright. The tag appears on the summon screen next to the grade, so it is a real classification, not marketing language.

    The pattern is worth reading before you spend. Every Alternative revealed so far sits at TSSR, and the top grade is almost entirely them. Crumble is not selling nostalgia at the top of the ladder; it is selling the multiverse variant of the character you already like, while the original returns further down.

    The six grades

    Crumble uses C, U, R, SR, SSR, TSSR. This is a new ladder for the franchise, not the Common through Ancient scale CookieRun: Kingdom players know, so Kingdom instincts and rate expectations do not transfer.

    TSSR The top grade. Almost entirely Alternative Cookies, the reimagined classics Crumble is built around, plus Wind Archer as the only straight returning unit at this tier.
    SSR The deepest and widest premium tier. Most of the recognizable later-era franchise cast sits here, plus two costume variants.
    SR Upper mid. Fifteen returning Cookies, mostly the fruit and specialist cast.
    R Lower mid. Notably includes the three Crumble Mercenary Guild leads, so your story protagonists are not premium pulls.
    U Uncommon. Eleven returning Cookies from the classic run era.
    C Common, and the base of the roster. GingerBrave, Strawberry Cookie and Wizard Cookie all return at the bottom tier, a real statement about where Crumble puts franchise nostalgia.
    The official CDN serves grade badge art for R, SSR and TSSR, and the site renders the TSSR badge next to Oven Wanderer Cookie, so those three are first-party. The badge URLs for C, U and SR return 404, so the bottom half of the ladder and every per-Cookie assignment below comes from the community wikis, not the developer. No source explains what the T in TSSR stands for.

    The eight Cookies the official site leads with

    The Cookies given full profiles on the official site. Three TSSR Alternatives, three Crumble Mercenary Guild leads, and two Implant Order officers. Note where the story protagonists sit on the ladder.

    Oven Wanderer Cookie

    TSSR

    Fire, Charge, Alternative

    The launch signature unit and the only Cookie whose full classification the developer has shown publicly. An alternate-universe GingerBrave, long lost in the Oven Labyrinth inside a dimensional rift, fighting with a candy cane sword carrying the flames of the Oven.

    GingerCraven

    TSSR

    Antagonist, Alternative

    Another GingerBrave from another universe, and the villain. Former dictator of the world Rancidia, now leading the Implant Order. Mixes tech with magic, lectures everyone about hypocrisy and bravery, and hates every GingerBrave in every universe. Himself included.

    Brightseeker Cookie

    TSSR

    Magi-engineer, Alternative

    A reimagining of the relentlessly cheerful GingerBright, older and no longer seeing only the bright side. Builds inventions around a lollipop, and her work made the Cookie world sweeter even if she has stopped saying so.

    Dark Cherry Cookie

    R

    Crumble Mercenary Guild

    Draws her sword first and reasons about it later. The blade is sharpened cherry blossom candy and leaves a tart cherry scent behind it. One of the three guild leads the story follows.

    Berry Yogurt Cookie

    R

    Crumble Mercenary Guild

    A former mansion maid turned mercenary. Gentle until money comes up, then explosive. He keeps the guild ledger, which in a story about debt is the most dangerous job in it.

    Grapevine Cookie

    R

    Crumble Mercenary Guild

    Excommunicated from an abbey for breaking one of its taboos. Chatters constantly over aged grape juice and occasionally drops something that turns out to matter.

    Cool Mint Cookie

    SSR

    Implant Order, added August 13

    Front-line prospector for the Implant Order. Follows the smell of expensive ore and shouts at anyone in her mines without a safety hat. Profiled as SSR before launch, absent from the day-one catalogue, and then the first Cookie added after it, arriving on August 13 at exactly the grade the profile promised. She is a Water Charge Cookie who digs up skulls to fight for her, and she is on both tier boards.

    Devil's Tooth Cookie

    SSR

    Implant Order, not in the roster yet

    Head strategist, accountant, and career counselor for the Order, all in one stoic package. Wants the Implant Order fortified beyond anyone's reach. Profiled as SSR pre-launch and still not in the catalogue. Cool Mint was the other one in that position and shipped two weeks after launch, so the pre-registration profiles are worth reading as a release plan rather than as cut content.
